newsitem.title: USA: NationsBank acquiring Boatmen's for $9.5 billion.
newsitem.headline: NationsBank acquiring Boatmen's for $9.5 billion.

text.p: NationsBank Corp. said Friday it agreed to acquire Boatmen's Bancshares Inc. for $9.5 billion, creating a financial giant stretching from North Carolina to New Mexico.
Investors greeted the news with mixed reactions, boosting Boatmen's shares by $10.6875 to $53.75 on the Nasdaq market and pushing NationsBank down $7.125 to $85.25 on the New York Stock Exchange .

The transaction, the third-biggest bank merger on record, will create a bank with $230 billion in assets, $20 billion in shareholders' equity and a market capitalisation of $33 billion, a joint announcement said.

The new company, with more than 13 million customers in 16 states, will become the country's fourth-largest commercial bank and have the potential to produce $3 billion in profits next year, the statement said.
NationsBank, with $192 billion in total assets, had been the fifth-largest U.S. commercial bank.

Analysts said NationsBank's Chairman Hugh McColl has proven again that he is one of the gutsiest acquirers in banking by paying a steep price to acquire Boatmen's Bancshares and extend his franchise into the U.S. heartland.
Although several analysts cut their ratings on NationsBank as its stock price fell, others said McColl was making a bold move to seize a unique opportunity.
"I think it's absolutely fabulous," said Robert Bonelli, executive vice president of Ernst & Co. and president of Ernst Asset Management.
"If you have to pay up for an organisation like Boatmen's, which happens to be one of the best-run banks in the country, you pay up for it. You don't get the opportunity every day," he said.

A key issue in the deal is the use of the purchase method of accounting instead of the more familiar pooling method. "Purchase accounting means you pay more in the short run but in the long run the actual cost to you is a lot less," said John Mason, an analyst at Interstate/Johnson Lane.
"Wells Fargo started the trend," said Emanuel Friedman of Friedman, Billings, Ramsey & Co. "The market is beginning to accept purchase accounting with large stock buybacks."
Under the deal, NationsBank, based in Charlotte, N.C., will exchange 0.6525 share of its common stock for each share of St.Louis-based Boatmen's, which has $41 billion in assets.
Based on Thursday's $92.375 closing price for NationsBank shares, the transaction will be worth $9.487 billion.
McColl told a news conference there will be "some" layoffs as a result of the merger with Boatmen's and also a hiring freeze across the entire company.
Some merger specialists expressed surprise at the amount NationsBank was offering, which represents a 40 percent premium over Boatmmen's closing price of $42.94 Thursday.
"What stunned me is the price," one said. "That's 2.7 times book value, and a premium like that has never been paid for a commercial bank. It's coming down to paying hefty premiums to consolidate."
The announcement said the deal will be structured as a "cash election" merger for Boatmen's shareholders, meaning they will have the right to receive either stock or cash.
The transaction will be a tax-free exchange for Boatmen's shareholders to the extent they receive shares of NationsBank, the companies said.
They added that at least 60 percent of the purchase price paid to all holders will be in NationsBank common stock. The balance will be paid in either cash or NationsBank stock, or a mix of the two.
NationsBank said it expected to realise $335 million in annual cost savings from the merger by 1999. This represents a reduction in combined expenses of 5 percent, it said.
The merger is subject to the approval of both companies' shareholders and the appropriate regulatory authorities.
